Without loss of generality, we assume that \delta\leq\delta_{0} and c_{1}<a-b. Let T_{2}:=\inf\{t\in\mathbb{N}^{*}:Y_{(1)}(t)-Y_{(2)}(t)\geq c_{1}\}. Note that when the event \mathcal{H}_{1} holds, we have T_{2}\leq C_{1}\log(n+1).
By Proposition 18, there exists a positive constant M\in\mathbb{N} that depends only on q,\beta,\delta, such that for any t\geq M and \bm{\alpha}\in\mathcal{X}_{c_{1}}, \|\Phi^{(t)}(\bm{\alpha})-\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{0}\|_{1}\leq\delta/\penalty 2, where \mathcal{X}_{c_{1}} and \Phi(\cdot) are as in Definition 12. We take
w_{1}:=\frac{\delta}{10\beta(2\beta q)^{M}},\quad w_{2}:=\frac{(1-\rho_{0})\delta}{5\sqrt{q}\beta^{2}},\quad w_{0}:=\min\{w_{1},w_{2}\},\quad\mathcal{D}_{3}:=\bigcap_{t=1}^{\lfloor K\log(n+1)\rfloor}\mathcal{E}_{t,w_{0},w_{0}},
where \mathcal{E}_{t,w_{0},w_{0}} is as in Definition 19.
Note that w_{1},w_{2},w_{0} depend only on q,\beta,\delta. By Lemma 20 and the union bound,
\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{D}_{3}^{c})\leq 4qK\log(n+1)\exp(-nw_{0}^{2}).
(44)
In the following, we assume that the event \mathcal{H}_{1}\cap\mathcal{D}_{3} holds. For any t\in\mathbb{N}, we let \gamma_{t}:=\Phi^{(t)}(s(\mathbf{Y}(T_{2}))). As s(\mathbf{Y}(T_{2}))\in\mathcal{X}_{c_{1}}, for any t\geq M,
\|\gamma_{t}-\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{0}\|_{1}=\|\Phi^{(t)}(s(\mathbf{Y}(T_{2})))-\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{0}\|_{1}\leq\frac{\delta}{2}.
(45)
For any t\in\mathbb{N} such that t\leq K\log(n+1), we have
\displaystyle\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\big(s_{\ell}(\mathbf{Y}(t+1))-\Phi_{\ell}(s(\mathbf{Y}(t)))\big)^{2}
\displaystyle\leq
\displaystyle 2\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\big(s_{\ell}(\mathbf{Y}(t+1))-\Phi_{\ell}(s(\mathbf{Z}(t)))\big)^{2}+2\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\big(\Phi_{\ell}(s(\mathbf{Z}(t)))-\Phi_{\ell}(s(\mathbf{Y}(t)))\big)^{2}
\displaystyle\leq
\displaystyle 2\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\big(\widetilde{Y}_{\ell}(t+1)-\Phi_{\ell}(\mathbf{Z}(t))\big)^{2}+2\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\big(\Phi_{\ell}(\mathbf{Z}(t))-\Phi_{\ell}(\mathbf{Y}(t))\big)^{2}
\displaystyle\leq
\displaystyle 2\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\big(\widetilde{Y}_{\ell}(t+1)-\Phi_{\ell}(\mathbf{Z}(t))\big)^{2}+2\big\|\Phi(\mathbf{Z}(t))-\Phi(\mathbf{Y}(t))\big\|_{1}^{2}
\displaystyle\leq
\displaystyle 2\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\big(\widetilde{Y}_{\ell}(t+1)-\Phi_{\ell}(\mathbf{Z}(t))\big)^{2}+8\beta^{2}q^{2}\|\mathbf{Z}(t)-\mathbf{Y}(t)\|_{\infty}^{2}\leq 2qw_{0}^{2}+8\beta^{2}q^{2}w_{0}^{2}\leq 10\beta^{4}w_{0}^{2},
where \tilde{Y}_{\ell}(t+1) is as in (31) and s_{\ell}(\mathbf{Y}(t+1)) is the \ellth component of s(\mathbf{Y}(t+1)), and we use the rearrangement inequality in the second inequality, Lemma 15 in the fourth inequality, and the fact that we are working on \mathcal{E}_{t,w_{0},w_{0}}\supseteq\mathcal{D}_{3} in the fifth inequality. Hence
\|s(\mathbf{Y}(t+1))-\Phi(s(\mathbf{Y}(t)))\|_{1}\leq\sqrt{q\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\big(s_{\ell}(\mathbf{Y}(t+1))-\Phi_{\ell}(s(\mathbf{Y}(t)))\big)^{2}}\leq 5\sqrt{q}\beta^{2}w_{0}.
(46)
For any t\in\mathbb{N} such that T_{2}+t\leq K\log(n+1), by (46) and Lemma 15,
\displaystyle\|s(\mathbf{Y}(T_{2}+t))-\gamma_{t}\|_{1}
\displaystyle\leq
\displaystyle\|s(\mathbf{Y}(T_{2}+t))-\Phi(s(\mathbf{Y}(T_{2}+t-1)))\|_{1}+\|\Phi(s(\mathbf{Y}(T_{2}+t-1)))-\Phi(\gamma_{t-1})\|_{1}
\displaystyle\leq
\displaystyle 5\sqrt{q}\beta^{2}w_{0}+2\beta q\|s(\mathbf{Y}(T_{2}+t-1))-\gamma_{t-1}\|_{1}.
Hence
\displaystyle\|s(\mathbf{Y}(T_{2}+t))-\gamma_{t}\|_{1}
\displaystyle\leq\|s(\mathbf{Y}(T_{2}+t))-\gamma_{t}\|_{1}+\frac{5\sqrt{q}\beta^{2}w_{0}}{2\beta q-1}
\displaystyle\leq 2\beta q\bigg(\|s(\mathbf{Y}(T_{2}+t-1))-\gamma_{t-1}\|_{1}+\frac{5\sqrt{q}\beta^{2}w_{0}}{2\beta q-1}\bigg).
By iterating the above inequality, noting that \gamma_{0}=s(\mathbf{Y}(T_{2})), we get
\displaystyle\|s(\mathbf{Y}(T_{2}+t))-\gamma_{t}\|_{1}
\displaystyle\leq(2\beta q)^{t}\Big(\|s(\mathbf{Y}(T_{2}))-\gamma_{0}\|_{1}+\frac{5\sqrt{q}\beta^{2}w_{0}}{2\beta q-1}\Big)
\displaystyle=\frac{5\sqrt{q}\beta^{2}}{2\beta q-1}(2\beta q)^{t}w_{0}\leq 5\beta(2\beta q)^{t}w_{0},
where the last inequality uses \beta>q\geq 2. By (45) and the above display, if T_{2}+M\leq K\log(n+1), then
\|s(\mathbf{Y}(T_{2}+M))-\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{0}\|_{1}\leq\|s(\mathbf{Y}(T_{2}+M))-\gamma_{M}\|_{1}+\|\gamma_{M}-\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{0}\|_{1}\leq 5\beta(2\beta q)^{M}w_{0}+\frac{\delta}{2}\leq\delta,
where the last inequality uses the choice of M and w_{0}.
Now we show by induction that for any t\in\mathbb{N} such that M\leq t\leq K\log(n+1)-T_{2}, we have \|s(\mathbf{Y}(T_{2}+t))-\bm{\alpha}_{0}\|_{1}\leq\delta. By the above display, this holds when t=M. Now we assume that M+1\leq t\leq K\log(n+1)-T_{2} and \|s(\mathbf{Y}(T_{2}+t-1))-\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{0}\|_{1}\leq\delta. Then, using the fact that \Phi(\bm{\alpha}_{0})=\bm{\alpha}_{0} (see Definition 14) and the triangle inequality, we get
\displaystyle\|s(\mathbf{Y}(T_{2}+t))-\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{0}\|_{1}=\|s(\mathbf{Y}(T_{2}+t))-\Phi(\bm{\alpha}_{0})\|_{1}
\displaystyle\leq
\displaystyle\|s(\mathbf{Y}(T_{2}+t))-\Phi(s(\mathbf{Y}(T_{2}+t-1)))\|_{1}+\|\Phi(s(\mathbf{Y}(T_{2}+t-1)))-\Phi(\bm{\alpha}_{0})\|_{1}
\displaystyle\leq
\displaystyle 5\sqrt{q}\beta^{2}w_{0}+\rho_{0}\|s(\mathbf{Y}(T_{2}+t-1))-\bm{\alpha}_{0}\|_{1}
\displaystyle\leq
\displaystyle(1-\rho_{0})\delta+\rho_{0}\delta\leq\delta,
where we use (46) with t replaced by t+T_{2}-1 and Lemma 16 in the third line, and the choice of w_{0} and the induction hypothesis in the fourth line. This proves the claim for all t\in\mathbb{N} such that M\leq t\leq K\log(n+1)-T_{2} by induction.
On the event \mathcal{H}_{1}, we have
T_{2}+M\leq C_{1}\log(n+1)+M\leq(C_{1}+1)\log(n+1),
(47)
where the second inequality holds for all n large enough (depending on q,\beta,\delta).
Hence for any t\in[(C_{1}+1)\log(n+1),K\log(n+1)]\cap\mathbb{N}, we have \mathcal{H}_{1}\cap\mathcal{D}_{3}\subseteq\mathcal{V}_{t,\delta}, and so (\mathcal{V}_{t,\delta})^{c}\cap\mathcal{H}_{1}\subseteq\mathcal{D}_{3}^{c}.
Consequently, by (44),
\mathbb{P}((\mathcal{V}_{t,\delta})^{c}\cap\mathcal{H}_{1})\leq\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{D}_{3}^{c})\leq 4qK\log(n+1)\exp(-nw_{0}^{2})\leq C^{\prime}\exp(-c^{\prime}n),
(48)
where C^{\prime},c^{\prime} are positive constants that depend only on q,\beta,K,\delta.
∎
6.4 Proof of Theorem 9
In this subsection, we complete the proof of Theorem 9. Consider any starting state \mathbf{X}(0)=(X_{1}(0),\cdots,X_{n}(0))\in[q]^{n}. Let \mathbf{X}^{\prime}(0)=(X^{\prime}_{1}(0),\cdots,X^{\prime}_{n}(0)) be drawn from the stationary distribution. For any t\in\mathbb{N}, we denote by \mathbf{X}(t) and \mathbf{X}^{\prime}(t) the states after running t steps of the modified AG sampler started from \mathbf{X}(0) and \mathbf{X}^{\prime}(0), respectively. For each t\in\mathbb{N} and \ell\in[q], we let
Y_{\ell}(t):=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}1\{X_{i}(t)=\ell\},\qquad Y^{\prime}_{\ell}(t):=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}1\{X^{\prime}_{i}(t)=\ell\}.
(49)
Let C_{1},c_{1} be defined as in Proposition 22. By a slight abuse of notation (see Definition 19), for any t\in\mathbb{N}, let \mathcal{F}_{t} be the \sigma-algebra generated by \{\mathbf{X}(s)\}_{s=0}^{t},\{\mathbf{Z}(s)\}_{s=0}^{t-1} and \{\mathbf{X}^{\prime}(s)\}_{s=0}^{t},\{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}(s)\}_{s=0}^{t-1}, and let \mathcal{G}_{t} be the \sigma-algebra generated by \{\mathbf{X}(s)\}_{s=0}^{t},\{\mathbf{Z}(s)\}_{s=0}^{t} and \{\mathbf{X}^{\prime}(s)\}_{s=0}^{t}, \{\mathbf{Z}^{\prime}(s)\}_{s=0}^{t}. Let \rho_{0},\delta_{0} be the constants in Lemma 16; note that \rho_{0},\delta_{0} only depend on q,\beta.
Below we construct a coupling between \mathbf{X}(t) and \mathbf{X}^{\prime}(t) for all t\in\mathbb{N}. For any t\in\mathbb{N}, given \mathbf{X}(t) and \mathbf{X}^{\prime}(t), we couple \mathbf{X}(t+1) and \mathbf{X}^{\prime}(t+1) as follows. Assume that Y_{\ell_{1}}(t)\geq Y_{\ell_{2}}(t)\geq\cdots\geq Y_{\ell_{q}}(t) and Y_{\ell_{1}^{\prime}}^{\prime}(t)\geq Y_{\ell_{2}^{\prime}}^{\prime}(t)\geq\cdots\geq Y_{\ell_{q}^{\prime}}^{\prime}(t) (where (\ell_{1},\cdots,\ell_{q}) and (\ell_{1}^{\prime},\cdots,\ell_{q}^{\prime}) are permutations of [q]). Let \lambda\in S_{q} be such that \lambda(\ell_{k})=\ell_{k}^{\prime} for each k\in[q]. For each \ell\in[q], we independently sample W_{\ell}(t)\sim N(0,(n\beta)^{-1}). Let
W^{\prime}_{\ell}(t)=W_{\lambda^{-1}(\ell)}(t),\qquad Z_{\ell}(t)=Y_{\ell}(t)+W_{\ell}(t),\qquad Z^{\prime}_{\ell}(t)=Y^{\prime}_{\ell}(t)+W^{\prime}_{\ell}(t).
(50)
For each i\in[n], we sample (\widetilde{X}_{i}(t+1),\widetilde{X}^{\prime}_{i}(t+1))\in[q]^{2} such that for each \ell\in[q],
\mathbb{P}(\widetilde{X}_{i}(t+1)=\ell|\mathcal{G}_{t})=\frac{e^{\beta Z_{\ell}(t)}}{\sum_{\ell^{\prime}=1}^{q}e^{\beta Z_{\ell^{\prime}}(t)}},\quad\mathbb{P}(\widetilde{X}^{\prime}_{i}(t+1)=\ell|\mathcal{G}_{t})=\frac{e^{\beta Z^{\prime}_{\ell}(t)}}{\sum_{\ell^{\prime}=1}^{q}e^{\beta Z^{\prime}_{\ell^{\prime}}(t)}},
and \mathbb{P}(\widetilde{X}_{i}(t+1)\neq\lambda^{-1}(\widetilde{X}^{\prime}_{i}(t+1))|\mathcal{G}_{t}) is equal to the total variation distance between the conditional laws of \widetilde{X}_{i}(t+1) and \lambda^{-1}(\widetilde{X}^{\prime}_{i}(t+1)) given \mathcal{G}_{t}. We sample \tau_{t} uniformly from S_{q}, and let \tau_{t}^{\prime}=\tau_{t}\lambda^{-1}\in S_{q}. Finally, set X_{i}(t+1)=\tau_{t}(\widetilde{X}_{i}(t+1)) and X^{\prime}_{i}(t+1)=\tau^{\prime}_{t}(\widetilde{X}^{\prime}_{i}(t+1)).
We fix K\geq 2(C_{1}+1), whose value will be determined later. We also let \delta=\delta_{0}/\penalty 2 and
\displaystyle t_{1}:=\lfloor C_{1}\log(n+1)\rfloor,\qquad t_{2}:=\lceil(C_{1}+1)\log(n+1)\rceil,\qquad t_{3}:=\lfloor K\log(n+1)\rfloor.
By another slight abuse of notation (see Proposition 22), let \mathcal{H}_{1} be the event that Y_{(1)}(t)-Y_{(2)}(t)\geq c_{1} for some t\in[t_{1}] and Y^{\prime}_{(1)}(t^{\prime})-Y^{\prime}_{(2)}(t^{\prime})\geq c_{1} for some t^{\prime}\in[t_{1}]. Note that \mathcal{H}_{1}\in\mathcal{F}_{t_{1}}, and by Proposition 22,
\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{H}_{1}^{c})\leq C\exp(-c\log\log(n+1)).
(51)
For any t\in\mathbb{N}, let \mathcal{V}_{t,\delta} be the event that \|s(\mathbf{Y}(t))-\bm{\alpha}_{0}\|_{1}\leq\delta and \|s(\mathbf{Y}^{\prime}(t))-\bm{\alpha}_{0}\|_{1}\leq\delta (where s(\mathbf{Y}(t)) and s(\mathbf{Y}^{\prime}(t)) are the order statistics of \mathbf{Y}(t) and \mathbf{Y}^{\prime}(t), respectively), and let \mathcal{U}_{t,\delta} be the event that \max_{\ell\in[q]}\{|W_{\ell}(t)|\}\leq\delta/\penalty q. Let \mathcal{W}_{K,\delta}:=\bigcap_{t\in[t_{2},t_{3}]\cap\mathbb{N}}\mathcal{V}_{t,\delta}.
By Proposition 23 and tail bounds for Gaussian random variables, we have
\mathbb{P}((\mathcal{W}_{K,\delta})^{c}\cap\mathcal{H}_{1})\leq C^{\prime}\exp(-c^{\prime}n),\quad\mathbb{P}((\mathcal{U}_{t,\delta})^{c})\leq 2q\exp(-n\beta q^{-2}\delta^{2}/\penalty 2)\leq C^{\prime}\exp(-c^{\prime}n),
(52)
where C^{\prime},c^{\prime} are positive constants that only depend on q,\beta,K.
Let H(\cdot,\cdot) be the Hamming distance on [q]^{n}. For any t\in\mathbb{N},
H(\mathbf{X}(t+1),\mathbf{X}^{\prime}(t+1))=\sum_{i=1}^{n}1\{X_{i}(t+1)\neq X^{\prime}_{i}(t+1)\}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}1\{\widetilde{X}_{i}(t+1)\neq\lambda^{-1}(\widetilde{X}^{\prime}_{i}(t+1))\},
hence
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[H(\mathbf{X}(t+1),\mathbf{X}^{\prime}(t+1))|\mathcal{F}_{t}]
\displaystyle=
\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{P}(\widetilde{X}_{i}(t+1)\neq\lambda^{-1}(\widetilde{X}^{\prime}_{i}(t+1))|\mathcal{F}_{t})
(53)
\displaystyle=
\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\mathbb{E}\bigg[\bigg|\frac{e^{\beta Z_{\ell}(t)}}{\sum_{\ell^{\prime}=1}^{q}e^{\beta Z_{\ell^{\prime}}(t)}}-\frac{e^{\beta Z^{\prime}_{\lambda(\ell)}(t)}}{\sum_{\ell^{\prime}=1}^{q}e^{\beta Z^{\prime}_{\ell^{\prime}}(t)}}\bigg|\bigg|\mathcal{F}_{t}\bigg],
where the last equality uses the fact that (\widetilde{X}_{i}(t+1),\lambda^{-1}(\widetilde{X}^{\prime}_{i}(t+1))) are coupled using the total variation coupling. Note that when \mathcal{U}_{t,\delta}\cap\mathcal{V}_{t,\delta} holds, we have
\displaystyle\|(Z_{\ell_{1}}(t),\cdots,Z_{\ell_{q}}(t))-\bm{\alpha}_{0}\|_{1}
\displaystyle\leq
\displaystyle\|(Z_{\ell_{1}}(t),\cdots,Z_{\ell_{q}}(t))-(Y_{\ell_{1}}(t),\cdots,Y_{\ell_{q}}(t))\|_{1}+\|s(\mathbf{Y}(t))-\bm{\alpha}_{0}\|_{1}
\displaystyle\leq
\displaystyle q\max_{\ell\in[q]}\{|W_{\ell}(t)|\}+\delta\leq 2\delta\leq\delta_{0}.
The same bound applies to (Z^{\prime}_{\ell_{1}^{\prime}}(t),\cdots,Z^{\prime}_{\ell_{q}^{\prime}}(t)), and consequently, on the set \mathcal{U}_{t,\delta}\cap\mathcal{V}_{t,\delta},
\displaystyle\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\bigg|\frac{e^{\beta Z_{\ell}(t)}}{\sum_{\ell^{\prime}=1}^{q}e^{\beta Z_{\ell^{\prime}}(t)}}-\frac{e^{\beta Z^{\prime}_{\lambda(\ell)}(t)}}{\sum_{\ell^{\prime}=1}^{q}e^{\beta Z^{\prime}_{\ell^{\prime}}(t)}}\bigg|
\displaystyle\leq
\displaystyle\rho_{0}\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}|Z_{\ell}(t)-Z^{\prime}_{\lambda(\ell)}(t)|=\rho_{0}\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}|Y_{\ell}(t)-Y^{\prime}_{\lambda(\ell)}(t)|
(54)
\displaystyle\leq
\displaystyle\rho_{0}\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}|Y_{\ell}(t)-Y^{\prime}_{\ell}(t)|\leq\frac{2}{n}\rho_{0}H(\mathbf{X}(t),\mathbf{X}^{\prime}(t)),
where the inequality in the first line uses
Lemma 16, the equality in the first line uses (50), the first inequality in the second line uses the fact that (Y_{\ell}(t))_{\ell\in[q]} and (Y^{\prime}_{\lambda(\ell)}(t))_{\ell\in[q]} have the same order, and the second inequality in the second line uses (49).
By (53) and (54), we have
\mathbb{E}[H(\mathbf{X}(t+1),\mathbf{X}^{\prime}(t+1))|\mathcal{F}_{t}]\leq\rho_{0}H(\mathbf{X}(t),\mathbf{X}^{\prime}(t))+\frac{nq}{2}(\mathbb{P}((\mathcal{U}_{t,\delta})^{c}|\mathcal{F}_{t})+\mathbb{P}((\mathcal{V}_{t,\delta})^{c}|\mathcal{F}_{t})).
For any t\in[t_{2},t_{3}]\cap\mathbb{N}, by (52), noting that \mathcal{H}_{1}\in\mathcal{F}_{t_{1}}\subseteq\mathcal{F}_{t}, we have
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[H(\mathbf{X}(t+1),\mathbf{X}^{\prime}(t+1))\mathbbm{1}_{\mathcal{H}_{1}}]=\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[H(\mathbf{X}(t+1),\mathbf{X}^{\prime}(t+1))|\mathcal{F}_{t}]\mathbbm{1}_{\mathcal{H}_{1}}]
\displaystyle\leq
\displaystyle\rho_{0}\mathbb{E}[H(\mathbf{X}(t),\mathbf{X}^{\prime}(t))\mathbbm{1}_{\mathcal{H}_{1}}]+\frac{nq}{2}(\mathbb{P}((\mathcal{U}_{t,\delta})^{c})+\mathbb{P}((\mathcal{V}_{t,\delta})^{c}\cap\mathcal{H}_{1}))
\displaystyle\leq
\displaystyle\rho_{0}\mathbb{E}[H(\mathbf{X}(t),\mathbf{X}^{\prime}(t))\mathbbm{1}_{\mathcal{H}_{1}}]+\frac{nq}{2}(\mathbb{P}((\mathcal{U}_{t,\delta})^{c})+\mathbb{P}((\mathcal{W}_{K,\delta})^{c}\cap\mathcal{H}_{1}))
\displaystyle\leq
\displaystyle\rho_{0}\mathbb{E}[H(\mathbf{X}(t),\mathbf{X}^{\prime}(t))\mathbbm{1}_{\mathcal{H}_{1}}]+C^{\prime}\exp(-c^{\prime}n).
Hence
\mathbb{E}[H(\mathbf{X}(t+1),\mathbf{X}^{\prime}(t+1))\mathbbm{1}_{\mathcal{H}_{1}}]-\frac{C^{\prime}\exp(-c^{\prime}n)}{1-\rho_{0}}\leq\rho_{0}\bigg(\mathbb{E}[H(\mathbf{X}(t),\mathbf{X}^{\prime}(t))\mathbbm{1}_{\mathcal{H}_{1}}]-\frac{C^{\prime}\exp(-c^{\prime}n)}{1-\rho_{0}}\bigg),
and consequently,
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[H(\mathbf{X}(t_{3}),\mathbf{X}^{\prime}(t_{3}))\mathbbm{1}_{\mathcal{H}_{1}}]-\frac{C^{\prime}\exp(-c^{\prime}n)}{1-\rho_{0}}
\displaystyle\leq\rho_{0}^{t_{3}-t_{2}}\bigg(\mathbb{E}[H(\mathbf{X}(t_{2}),\mathbf{X}^{\prime}(t_{2}))\mathbbm{1}_{\mathcal{H}_{1}}]-\frac{C^{\prime}\exp(-c^{\prime}n)}{1-\rho_{0}}\bigg)
\displaystyle\leq\rho_{0}^{t_{3}-t_{2}}n\leq\rho_{0}^{K\log(n+1)/\penalty 3}n,
where the last inequality holds for all n large enough (depending on q,\beta,K). Taking K sufficiently large (depending on q,\beta) and n sufficiently large (depending on q,\beta,K), by (51) and the above display, we get
\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{H}_{1}^{c})\leq\frac{1}{8},\qquad\mathbb{P}(\{\mathbf{X}(t_{3})\neq\mathbf{X}^{\prime}(t_{3})\}\cap\mathcal{H}_{1})\leq\mathbb{E}[H(\mathbf{X}(t_{3}),\mathbf{X}^{\prime}(t_{3}))\mathbbm{1}_{\mathcal{H}_{1}}]\leq\frac{1}{8}.
(55)
Hence \mathbb{P}(\mathbf{X}(t_{3})\neq\mathbf{X}^{\prime}(t_{3}))\leq\frac{1}{4}.
Thus by the coupling lemma (Levin and Peres, 2017, Theorem 5.4), t_{\mathrm{mix}}\Big(\frac{1}{4}\Big)\leq t_{3}\leq C\log(n+1).
By (Levin and Peres, 2017, (4.34)), we obtain the conclusion of the theorem.
7 Discussion
This paper builds on a growing literature on sampling methods for Ising and Potts models, using an auxiliary Gaussian variable, a strategy first proposed in the machine learning literature by Martens and Sutskever (2010).
We present two novel choices of auxiliary Gaussian variables: (i) a choice for Potts models, which leads to a sampler whose cost per iteration scales linearly in q; and (ii) a choice which automatically detects the (approximately) low-rank structure of \bf A and takes advantage of this low-rank structure, if it exists.
We primarily focus on the AG sampler, which is a block Gibbs sampler.
We run an extensive suite of numerical experiments and identify many regimes where the AG sampler outperforms competitors, at times yielding an ESS/s which is orders of magnitudes higher—for example for Ising models on a graph and low-rank Hopfield networks.
We also identify regimes where the AG sampler exhibits poor performance, for example when applied to a cold spin glass system.
Overall, we believe that the AG sampler’s ease of implementation and competitive performance make it an excellent method to sample from Potts models.
Our paper also provides bounds on the mixing time of AG samplers.
Such bounds exist for the Heat Bath and Swendsen-Wang algorithms.
To the best of our knowledge, our paper provides the first bounds for AG samplers. Our bounds are of similar order as those for Swendsen-Wang algorithms (see, e.g., Galanis et al. (2019)).
There exist several directions for future research. First, it would be of interest to establish matching lower bounds on the mixing time for Theorems 5 and 9. Second, it would be interesting to extend Theorem 9 to the low-temperature regime for broader classes of models, such as Potts models on random regular graphs. Another direction for future research is to investigate other algorithms which use the auxiliary Gaussian variables we propose.
This includes discrete HMC (Zhang et al., 2012) and more generally gradient-based methods to sample over \bf Z.
An important challenge here is to understand the geometry of p({\bf Z}) and which methods—or which tuning of a method—enable efficient sampling.
Similarly, it is of interest to study how tempering best works with an AG sampler, or any sampler over \mathbb{P}({\bf X},{\bf Z}) in order to sample from cold systems.

SM gratefully acknowledges NSF for partial support during this research (DMS-2113414, DMS-2515519).
Appendix
The Appendix contains proofs missing in the main body.
We derive the conditional and marginal distributions, that arise when we introduce either a regular or low-rank auxiliary Gaussian variable for Potts models.
We prove Proposition 3, which characterizes the error committed in using the low-rank algorithm, and Proposition 4, which characterizes the type of coupling matrices for which we may want to use a low-rank algorithm.
Specialized algorithms for the Ising model (q=2) are derived. We also provide an overview on auxiliary cluster and tempering algorithms.
The code used for our numerical experiments can be found at https://github.com/charlesm93/potts_simulation.
The ReadMe provides instructions on how to run the code.
Appendix A Missing proofs in Section 2
A.1 Conditional and marginal distributions when using the regular Auxiliary Gaussian
We begin by proving Equations (6) and (7).
Recall from (4) that the marginal p.m.f. of \mathbf{X} under \mathbb{P} is proportional to
\exp\Big(\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}{\bf y}_{\ell}^{\prime}B{\bf y}_{\ell}\Big).
Also from (5), the conditional density of \mathbf{Z} given \mathbf{X}=\mathbf{x} is proportional to
\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}(\mathbf{z}_{\ell}-\mathbf{y}_{\ell})^{\prime}B(\mathbf{z}_{\ell}-\mathbf{y}_{\ell})\Big).
Thus, the joint distribution of \mathbf{X} and \mathbf{Z} is proportional to
\displaystyle\exp\left(\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\Big[{\bf y}_{\ell}^{\prime}B{\bf y}_{\ell}-(\mathbf{z}_{\ell}-\mathbf{y}_{\ell})^{\prime}B(\mathbf{z}_{\ell}-\mathbf{y}_{\ell})\Big]\right)
\displaystyle=
\displaystyle\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\mathbf{z}_{\ell}^{\prime}B\mathbf{z}_{\ell}+\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\mathbf{z}_{\ell}^{\prime}B\mathbf{y}_{\ell}\right)
\displaystyle=
\displaystyle\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\mathbf{z}_{\ell}^{\prime}B\mathbf{z}_{\ell}+\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}z_{\ell j}B_{ij}1\{x_{i}=\ell\}\right).
(56)
From (56), we see that given \mathbf{Z}, the random variables (X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}) are mutually independent, with
\mathbb{P}(X_{i}=\ell|\mathbf{Z})\propto\exp\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{n}B_{ij}z_{\ell j}\Big),
which verifies (6).
The marginal distribution of \mathbf{Z} is obtained from (56) by summing over \mathbf{x}\in[q]^{n}, from which (7) follows.
A.2 Conditional and marginal distributions when using the low-rank Auxiliary Gaussian
Next we prove Equations (13) and (15).
Recall from (12) that the marginal p.m.f. of \mathbf{X} under \mathbb{P} is proportional to
\exp\Big(\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\sum_{j=1}^{k}\mu_{j}(\mathbf{p}_{j}^{\prime}y_{\ell})^{2}\Big).
Also from (13), the conditional density of \mathbf{Z} given \mathbf{X}=\mathbf{x} is proportional to
\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\sum_{j=1}^{k}\mu_{j}(z_{\ell j}-\mathbf{p}_{j}^{\prime}\mathbf{y}_{\ell})^{2}\Big).
Thus, the joint distribution of \mathbf{X} and \mathbf{Z} is proportional to
\displaystyle\exp\left(\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\sum_{j=1}^{k}\mu_{j}\Big[(\mathbf{p}_{j}^{\prime}y_{\ell})^{2}-(z_{\ell j}-\mathbf{p}_{j}^{\prime}\mathbf{y}_{\ell})^{2}\Big]\right)
\displaystyle=
\displaystyle\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\sum_{j=1}^{k}\mu_{j}z_{\ell j}^{2}+\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\sum_{j=1}^{k}\mu_{j}z_{\ell j}\mathbf{p}_{j}^{\prime}\mathbf{y}_{\ell}\Big)
\displaystyle=
\displaystyle\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\sum_{j=1}^{k}\mu_{j}z_{\ell j}^{2}+\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\sum_{j=1}^{k}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mu_{j}z_{\ell j}p_{ji}1\{x_{i}=\ell\}\Big).
(57)
Using (57), given \mathbf{Z}=\mathbf{z} the random variables (X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}) are mutually independent, with
\mathbb{P}(X_{i}=\ell|\mathbf{Z})\propto\exp\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{k}\mu_{j}z_{\ell j}p_{ji}\Big),
which verifies (14). The marginal distribution of \mathbf{Z} is obtained from (57) by summing over \mathbf{x}\in[q]^{n}, from which (15) follows.
A.3 Proof of Proposition 3
With B and \tilde{B} as in the distributions \mathbb{P} and \mathbb{Q} in (4)
and (11) respectively, for any \mathbf{x}\in[q]^{n}, we have
\displaystyle\Big|\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}B_{ij}1\{x_{i}=x_{j}\}-\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}\tilde{B}_{ij}1\{x_{i}=x_{j}\}\Big|=
\displaystyle\Big|\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\mathbf{y}_{\ell}^{\prime}(B-\tilde{B})\mathbf{y}_{\ell}\Big|
\displaystyle\leq
\displaystyle\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\|\mathbf{y}_{\ell}\|_{2}^{2}\|B-\tilde{B}\|_{2}
\displaystyle=
\displaystyle\|B-\tilde{B}\|_{2}\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\sum_{i=1}^{n}1\{x_{i}=\ell\}
(58)
\displaystyle=
\displaystyle n\|B-\tilde{B}\|_{2}\leq n\varepsilon,
(59)
where the last bound uses the definition of \tilde{B} to note that all eigenvalues of B-\tilde{B} are smaller than \varepsilon in absolute value.
Thus, for any \mathbf{x}\in[q]^{n}, we have
\displaystyle e^{\frac{-n\beta\varepsilon}{2}}\leq\frac{\exp\Big(\frac{\beta}{2}\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}B_{ij}1\{x_{i}=x_{j}\}\Big)}{\exp\Big(\frac{\beta}{2}\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}\tilde{B}_{ij}1\{x_{i}=x_{j}\}\Big)}\leq e^{\frac{n\beta\varepsilon}{2}}.
(60)
On summing over \mathbf{x}\in[q]^{n}, this gives
\displaystyle e^{-\frac{n\beta\varepsilon}{2}}\leq\frac{Z(\beta,B)}{Z(\beta,\tilde{B})}\leq e^{\frac{n\beta\varepsilon}{2}},
(61)
which verifies part (i). For verifying part (ii), taking a ratio of (60) and (61) we get
\displaystyle e^{-n\beta\varepsilon}\leq\frac{\mathbb{P}(\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{x})}{\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{x})}\leq e^{n\beta\varepsilon},
which gives
\max({\rm KL}(\mathbb{P}|\mathbb{Q}),{\rm KL}(\mathbb{Q}|\mathbb{P}))\leq n\beta\varepsilon. This verifies part (ii), and hence completes the proof of the lemma.
A.4 Proof of Proposition 4
To begin, we bound k by examining the trace of B^{2}, and noting that, per Markov’s inequality,
k\leq\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mu_{i}^{2}/\varepsilon^{2}={\rm tr}(B^{2})/\varepsilon^{2}.
Also, we have
\displaystyle{\rm tr}(B^{2})=\beta^{2}{\rm tr}(A^{2}+2|\lambda_{\min}|A+\lambda_{\min}^{2}I)=\beta^{2}{\rm tr}(A^{2})+\beta^{2}n\lambda_{\min}^{2}.
(62)
Combining the above two displays, it suffices to show that the RHS of (62) is o(n).
Since \lambda_{\min}=o(1), it suffices to show {\rm tr}(A^{2})=o(n), which is the focus of the rest of the proof.
To this effect, recall that {\rm tr}(A)=0. Thus, with \lambda_{1}(A),\ldots,\lambda_{n}(A) denoting the eigenvalues of A we have
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}(A)1\{\lambda_{i}(A)>0\}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}|\lambda_{i}(A)|1\{\lambda_{i}(A)<0\}\leq n|\lambda_{\min}|.
This in turn gives
\sum_{i=1}^{n}|\lambda_{i}(A)|=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}(A)1\{\lambda_{i}(A)>0\}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}|\lambda_{i}(A)|1\{\lambda_{i}(A)<0\}\leq 2n|\lambda_{\min}|=o(n),
and so
{\rm tr}(A^{2})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}(A)^{2}\leq\max\{|\lambda_{\max}|,|\lambda_{\min}|\}\sum_{i=1}^{n}|\lambda_{i}(A)|=o(n),
where the last equality uses the assumption that \lambda_{\max}=O(1) and \lambda_{\min}=o(1). This completes the proof of the proposition.
Appendix B Missing proofs in Section 6
B.1 Proof of Lemma 13
For any x\in[0,1], let \psi(x):=(1-x)e^{\beta x}-(q-1)x-1, and note that
\displaystyle\psi(0)=0,\qquad\psi^{\prime}(x)=-e^{\beta x}+\beta e^{\beta x}(1-x)-(q-1),\qquad\psi^{\prime\prime}(x)=\beta e^{\beta x}(\beta(1-x)-2).
Then \psi^{\prime\prime}(x) has exactly one root in [0,1], and so \psi^{\prime}(x) has at most two roots in [0,1]. As \psi^{\prime}(0)=\beta-q>0 and \psi^{\prime}(1)=-e^{\beta}-q+1<0, there exists a unique root for \psi^{\prime}(x) in (0,1), which we denote by x_{1}. Since \psi(x) is strictly increasing on [0,x_{1}) with \psi(x_{1})>\psi(0)=0, and strictly decreasing on (x_{1},1] with \psi(1)=-q<0, it follows that there exists a unique x_{0}\in(x_{1},1), such that \psi(x_{0})=0. Also, recalling the formulas of \psi,g, we can write \psi(x)=(e^{\beta x}-1)\big(1-\frac{x}{g(x)}\big). Consequently, this gives
\displaystyle g(0)=0;\quad g(x_{0})=x_{0};\quad g(x)>x\text{ for }x\in(0,x_{0});\quad g(x)<x\text{ for }x\in(x_{0},1].
(63)
We now give the proof of part (a). Suppose (x,y) is an arbitrary solution of (29), if it exists. Then we have x-y\in(0,1) and
g(x-y)=\frac{e^{\beta(x-y)}-1}{e^{\beta(x-y)}+q-1}=\frac{x/\penalty y-1}{x/\penalty y+q-1}=\frac{x-y}{x+(q-1)y}=x-y.
Since g has a unique fixed point x_{0} in (0,1), we have x-y=x_{0}. As x+(q-1)y=1, solving this we get x=(1+(q-1)x_{0})/\penalty q and y=(1-x_{0})/\penalty q. Thus there is at most a unique solution to (29). The fact that x=(1+(q-1)x_{0})/\penalty q and y=(1-x_{0})/\penalty q is a solution can be verified by elementary computations. As a-b=x_{0}>x_{1}, by the above analysis, \psi^{\prime}(a-b)<0, which yields -e^{\beta(a-b)}+\beta e^{\beta(a-b)}(1-a+b)-(q-1)<0. This, along with (29), gives
\displaystyle 0>-\frac{a}{b}+\beta\cdot\frac{a}{b}\cdot qb-(q-1)=-\frac{a}{b}+\beta aq-(q-1)\Rightarrow\beta qab<a+(q-1)b=1.
This completes the proof of part (a).
Part (b) now follows from part (a) and (63), on noting that a-b=x_{0}.
Turning to the proof of part (c),
note that for any x\in[q^{-1},1],
\displaystyle h(x)>x\Leftrightarrow(1-x)e^{\beta x}>x(q-1)e^{\beta\frac{1-x}{q-1}}\Leftrightarrow(1-x)e^{\beta\frac{qx-1}{q-1}}>x(q-1),
\displaystyle g\bigg(\frac{qx-1}{q-1}\bigg)>\frac{qx-1}{q-1}\Leftrightarrow(q-1)\Big(e^{\beta\frac{qx-1}{q-1}}-1\Big)>(qx-1)\Big(e^{\beta\frac{qx-1}{q-1}}+q-1\Big)\Leftrightarrow(1-x)e^{\beta\frac{qx-1}{q-1}}>x(q-1).
Thus we conclude that h(x)>x if and only if g\Big(\frac{qx-1}{q-1}\Big)>\frac{qx-1}{q-1}. When x\in(q^{-1},a), we have \frac{qx-1}{q-1}\in\big(0,\frac{qa-1}{q-1}\big)=(0,a-b); using part (b) and the above conclusion, we have h(x)>x when x\in(q^{-1},a). Similarly, we can deduce that h(a)=a and h(x)<x when x\in(a,1]. The fact that h(q^{-1})=q^{-1} follows from direct computation.
B.2 Proof of Lemma 15
For any \ell\in[q] and \theta\in[0,1], let
\phi_{\ell}(\theta)=\Phi_{\ell}(\theta\bm{\alpha}+(1-\theta)\bm{\alpha}^{\prime})=\frac{e^{\beta(\theta\alpha_{\ell}+(1-\theta)\alpha_{\ell}^{\prime})}}{\sum_{\ell^{\prime}=1}^{q}e^{\beta(\theta\alpha_{\ell^{\prime}}+(1-\theta)\alpha_{\ell^{\prime}}^{\prime})}}.
(64)
Note that
\phi_{\ell}^{\prime}(\theta)=\frac{\beta e^{\beta(\theta\alpha_{\ell}+(1-\theta)\alpha^{\prime}_{\ell})}\sum_{\ell^{\prime}\in[q]\backslash\{\ell\}}e^{\beta(\theta\alpha_{\ell^{\prime}}+(1-\theta)\alpha^{\prime}_{\ell^{\prime}})}\big((\alpha_{\ell}-\alpha_{\ell}^{\prime})-(\alpha_{\ell^{\prime}}-\alpha^{\prime}_{\ell^{\prime}})\big)}{\big(\sum_{\ell^{\prime}=1}^{q}e^{\beta(\theta\alpha_{\ell^{\prime}}+(1-\theta)\alpha_{\ell^{\prime}}^{\prime})}\big)^{2}}.
Hence |\phi^{\prime}_{\ell}(\theta)|\leq 2\beta\max_{\ell^{\prime}\in[q]}|\alpha^{\prime}_{\ell^{\prime}}-\alpha_{\ell^{\prime}}|.
Therefore,
\|\Phi(\bm{\alpha^{\prime}})-\Phi(\bm{\alpha})\|_{1}=\sum_{\ell\in[q]}|\phi_{\ell}(1)-\phi_{\ell}(0)|\leq 2\beta q\max_{\ell^{\prime}\in[q]}|\alpha^{\prime}_{\ell^{\prime}}-\alpha_{\ell^{\prime}}|.
B.3 Proof of Lemma 16
For any \bm{\alpha}=(\alpha_{1},\cdots,\alpha_{q})\in\mathbb{R}^{q},
\frac{\partial\Phi_{\ell}(\bm{\alpha})}{\partial\alpha_{\ell}}=\frac{\beta e^{\beta\alpha_{\ell}}\big(\sum_{s\in[q]\backslash\{\ell\}}e^{\beta\alpha_{s}}\big)}{\big(\sum_{s=1}^{q}e^{\beta\alpha_{s}}\big)^{2}},\quad\forall\ell\in[q],
\frac{\partial\Phi_{\ell}(\bm{\alpha})}{\partial\alpha_{\ell^{\prime}}}=\frac{-\beta e^{\beta\alpha_{\ell}}e^{\beta\alpha_{\ell^{\prime}}}}{\big(\sum_{s=1}^{q}e^{\beta\alpha_{s}}\big)^{2}},\quad\forall\ell,\ell^{\prime}\in[q]\text{ such that }\ell\neq\ell^{\prime}.
In particular, with \boldsymbol{\alpha}_{0} as in Definition 14, we have
\frac{\partial\Phi_{1}(\bm{\alpha}_{0})}{\partial\alpha_{1}}=\frac{\beta(q-1)e^{\beta a}e^{\beta b}}{(e^{\beta a}+(q-1)e^{\beta b})^{2}},
(65)
\frac{\partial\Phi_{\ell}(\bm{\alpha}_{0})}{\partial\alpha_{\ell}}=\frac{\beta e^{\beta b}(e^{\beta a}+(q-2)e^{\beta b})}{(e^{\beta a}+(q-1)e^{\beta b})^{2}},\quad\forall\ell\in[q]\backslash\{1\},
(66)
\frac{\partial\Phi_{\ell}(\bm{\alpha}_{0})}{\partial\alpha_{\ell^{\prime}}}=\frac{-\beta e^{\beta a}e^{\beta b}}{(e^{\beta a}+(q-1)e^{\beta b})^{2}},\quad\forall\ell,\ell^{\prime}\in[q]\text{ such that }\ell\neq\ell^{\prime}\text{ and }\min\{\ell,\ell^{\prime}\}=1,
(67)
\frac{\partial\Phi_{\ell}(\bm{\alpha}_{0})}{\partial\alpha_{\ell^{\prime}}}=\frac{-\beta e^{2\beta b}}{(e^{\beta a}+(q-1)e^{\beta b})^{2}},\quad\forall\ell,\ell^{\prime}\in[q]\text{ such that }\ell\neq\ell^{\prime}\text{ and }\min\{\ell,\ell^{\prime}\}\geq 2.
(68)
For any \ell,i,j\in[q] such that i<j, we bound \sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\big|\frac{\partial\Phi_{\ell}(\bm{\alpha}_{0})}{\partial\alpha_{i}}-\frac{\partial\Phi_{\ell}(\bm{\alpha}_{0})}{\partial\alpha_{j}}\big| as follows. If i=1, then j\in[q]\backslash\{1\}, and using (65)–(68), we get
\displaystyle\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\bigg|\frac{\partial\Phi_{\ell}(\bm{\alpha}_{0})}{\partial\alpha_{i}}-\frac{\partial\Phi_{\ell}(\bm{\alpha}_{0})}{\partial\alpha_{j}}\bigg|
\displaystyle=\,
\displaystyle\bigg|\frac{\partial\Phi_{1}(\bm{\alpha}_{0})}{\partial\alpha_{1}}-\frac{\partial\Phi_{1}(\bm{\alpha}_{0})}{\partial\alpha_{j}}\bigg|+\bigg|\frac{\partial\Phi_{j}(\bm{\alpha}_{0})}{\partial\alpha_{1}}-\frac{\partial\Phi_{j}(\bm{\alpha}_{0})}{\partial\alpha_{j}}\bigg|+\sum_{\ell\in[q]\backslash\{1,j\}}\bigg|\frac{\partial\Phi_{\ell}(\bm{\alpha}_{0})}{\partial\alpha_{1}}-\frac{\partial\Phi_{\ell}(\bm{\alpha}_{0})}{\partial\alpha_{j}}\bigg|
\displaystyle=\,
\displaystyle\frac{|\beta(q-1)e^{\beta a}e^{\beta b}+\beta e^{\beta a}e^{\beta b}|+|-\beta e^{\beta a}e^{\beta b}-\beta e^{\beta b}(e^{\beta a}+(q-2)e^{\beta b})|}{(e^{\beta a}+(q-1)e^{\beta b})^{2}}
\displaystyle+\frac{(q-2)|-\beta e^{\beta a}e^{\beta b}+\beta e^{2\beta b}|}{(e^{\beta a}+(q-1)e^{\beta b})^{2}}
\displaystyle=\,
\displaystyle\frac{\beta qe^{\beta a}e^{\beta b}+\beta e^{\beta b}(2e^{\beta a}+(q-2)e^{\beta b})+(q-2)\beta e^{\beta b}(e^{\beta a}-e^{\beta b})}{(e^{\beta a}+(q-1)e^{\beta b})^{2}}=\frac{2\beta qe^{\beta a}e^{\beta b}}{(e^{\beta a}+(q-1)e^{\beta b})^{2}}
\displaystyle=\,
\displaystyle\frac{2\beta qab}{(a+(q-1)b)^{2}}=2q\beta ab,
(69)
where we use (29) in the last two equalities. Next, if i\geq 2, then i,j\in[q]\backslash\{1\}, and using (66)–(68), we get
\displaystyle\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\bigg|\frac{\partial\Phi_{\ell}(\bm{\alpha}_{0})}{\partial\alpha_{i}}-\frac{\partial\Phi_{\ell}(\bm{\alpha}_{0})}{\partial\alpha_{j}}\bigg|=\bigg|\frac{\partial\Phi_{i}(\bm{\alpha}_{0})}{\partial\alpha_{i}}-\frac{\partial\Phi_{i}(\bm{\alpha}_{0})}{\partial\alpha_{j}}\bigg|+\bigg|\frac{\partial\Phi_{j}(\bm{\alpha}_{0})}{\partial\alpha_{i}}-\frac{\partial\Phi_{j}(\bm{\alpha}_{0})}{\partial\alpha_{j}}\bigg|
\displaystyle=\,
\displaystyle\frac{2|\beta e^{\beta b}(e^{\beta a}+(q-2)e^{\beta b})+\beta e^{2\beta b}|}{(e^{\beta a}+(q-1)e^{\beta b})^{2}}=\frac{2\beta e^{\beta b}}{e^{\beta a}+(q-1)e^{\beta b}}=\frac{2\beta b}{a+(q-1)b}=2\beta b\leq 2q\beta ab,
(70)
where we use (29) in the last two equalities and Lemma 13(a) in the inequality in the second line.
Below we consider any \bm{\alpha},\bm{\alpha}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{q} such that \sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\alpha_{\ell}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\alpha_{\ell}^{\prime}. For any \ell\in[q], let
H_{\ell}(\bm{\alpha},\bm{\alpha}^{\prime}):=\sum_{\ell^{\prime}=1}^{q}(\alpha_{\ell^{\prime}}-\alpha^{\prime}_{\ell^{\prime}})\frac{\partial\Phi_{\ell}(\bm{\alpha}_{0})}{\partial\alpha_{\ell^{\prime}}}.
(71)
We bound \sum_{\ell=1}^{q}|H_{\ell}(\bm{\alpha},\bm{\alpha}^{\prime})| as follows. Without loss of generality, we assume that \bm{\alpha}\neq\bm{\alpha}^{\prime}. Let I_{+}:=\{\ell\in[q]:\alpha_{\ell}>\alpha^{\prime}_{\ell}\} and I_{-}:=\{\ell\in[q]:\alpha_{\ell}<\alpha^{\prime}_{\ell}\}. As \sum_{\ell\in I_{+}}(\alpha_{\ell}-\alpha^{\prime}_{\ell})=\sum_{\ell\in I_{-}}(\alpha^{\prime}_{\ell}-\alpha_{\ell}), there exists a finite sequence \{\bm{\alpha}_{j}\}_{j=0}^{J} (where J\in\mathbb{N}^{*}) from \mathbb{R}^{q}, such that \bm{\alpha}_{0}=\bm{\alpha}, \bm{\alpha}_{J}=\bm{\alpha}^{\prime}, and for any j\in[0,J-1]\cap\mathbb{N}, there exists some \ell_{j},\ell_{j}^{\prime}\in[q], such that \ell_{j}\neq\ell_{j}^{\prime}, (\bm{\alpha}_{j})_{\ell_{j}}>(\bm{\alpha}_{j+1})_{\ell_{j}}, (\bm{\alpha}_{j})_{\ell_{j}^{\prime}}<(\bm{\alpha}_{j+1})_{\ell_{j}^{\prime}}, (\bm{\alpha}_{j})_{\ell_{j}}-(\bm{\alpha}_{j+1})_{\ell_{j}}=(\bm{\alpha}_{j+1})_{\ell_{j}^{\prime}}-(\bm{\alpha}_{j})_{\ell_{j}^{\prime}}, and (\bm{\alpha}_{j})_{\ell}=(\bm{\alpha}_{j+1})_{\ell} for any \ell\in[q]\backslash\{\ell_{j},\ell_{j}^{\prime}\}. Moreover, letting s_{j}=(\bm{\alpha}_{j})_{\ell_{j}}-(\bm{\alpha}_{j+1})_{\ell_{j}}, we can select the sequence so that
\sum_{j=0}^{J-1}s_{j}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}|\bm{\alpha}_{\ell}-\bm{\alpha}^{\prime}_{\ell}|.
(72)
For any j\in[0,J-1]\cap\mathbb{N}, using (71) we have
\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}|H_{\ell}(\bm{\alpha}_{j},\bm{\alpha}_{j+1})|=s_{j}\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\bigg|\frac{\partial\Phi_{\ell}(\bm{\alpha}_{0})}{\partial\alpha_{\ell_{j}}}-\frac{\partial\Phi_{\ell}(\bm{\alpha}_{0})}{\partial\alpha_{\ell_{j}^{\prime}}}\bigg|\leq 2q\beta abs_{j},
where the last inequality uses (69) and (70). Hence by the above display and (72), we have
\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}|H_{\ell}(\bm{\alpha},\bm{\alpha}^{\prime})|\leq\sum_{j=0}^{J-1}\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}|H_{\ell}(\bm{\alpha}_{j},\bm{\alpha}_{j+1})|\leq 2q\beta ab\sum_{j=0}^{J-1}s_{j}=q\beta ab\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}|\bm{\alpha}_{\ell}-\bm{\alpha}^{\prime}_{\ell}|.
We define \phi_{\ell}(\theta) for any \ell\in[q] and \theta\in[0,1] as in (64). For any \ell\in[q],
\displaystyle\Phi_{\ell}(\bm{\alpha})-\Phi_{\ell}(\bm{\alpha}^{\prime})
\displaystyle=
\displaystyle\phi_{\ell}(1)-\phi_{\ell}(0)=\int_{0}^{1}\phi_{\ell}^{\prime}(\theta)d\theta
\displaystyle=
\displaystyle\sum_{\ell^{\prime}=1}^{q}(\alpha_{\ell^{\prime}}-\alpha^{\prime}_{\ell^{\prime}})\int_{0}^{1}\frac{\partial\Phi_{\ell}(\theta\bm{\alpha}+(1-\theta)\bm{\alpha}^{\prime})}{\partial\alpha_{\ell^{\prime}}}d\theta.
By Lemma 13(a), q\beta ab<1. The conclusion of the lemma follows from the above two displays, on using the continuity of \nabla\Phi.
B.4 Proof of Lemma 17
Note that \Phi_{1}(\bm{\alpha})-\Phi_{2}(\bm{\alpha})=\frac{e^{\beta\alpha_{1}}-e^{\beta\alpha_{2}}}{\sum_{k=1}^{q}e^{\beta\alpha_{k}}}\geq\frac{e^{\beta\alpha_{1}}-e^{\beta\alpha_{2}}}{e^{\beta\alpha_{1}}+(q-1)e^{\beta\alpha_{2}}}=g(\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2}), where g is defined as in Lemma 13(b). To complete the proof, note that for any x\geq 0,
g^{\prime}(x)=\frac{q\beta e^{\beta x}}{(e^{\beta x}+q-1)^{2}}>0,
hence g^{\prime}(0)=\beta/\penalty q and g is monotone increasing on [0,\infty). Moreover, we have g(0)=0 (see Lemma 13(b)).
Let \delta=\delta_{\beta,q,\rho}>0 be such that g^{\prime}(x)>\rho\beta/\penalty q for x\in[0,\delta], the existence of which follows from the continuity of g^{\prime}. Then, if \alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2}<\delta, we have
\displaystyle g(\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2})=g(\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2})-g(0)\geq\rho\beta q^{-1}(\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2}).
On the other hand, if \alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2}\geq\delta, then
\displaystyle g(\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2})\geq g(\delta)=:\kappa_{\rho},
where \kappa_{\rho} depends only on q,\beta,\rho. The conclusion of the lemma follows by combining the above two displays.
Appendix C Specialized Auxiliary Gaussian algorithm for q=2
C.1 Standard Auxiliary Gaussian algorithm
Setting \mathbf{W}:=\mathbf{Z}_{1}-\mathbf{Z}_{2} and using (5), under \mathbb{P} we have
\displaystyle(\mathbf{W}|\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{x})\sim N(\mathbf{y}_{1}-\mathbf{y}_{2},2B^{-1}).
(73)
Also, using (6), we have
\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(X_{i}=1|\mathbf{Z}=\mathbf{z})=
\displaystyle\frac{\exp\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{n}B_{ij}z_{1j}\Big)}{\exp\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{n}B_{ij}z_{1j}\Big)+\exp\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{n}B_{ij}z_{2j}\Big)}
\displaystyle=
\displaystyle\frac{\exp\Big(\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{n}B_{ij}w_{j}\Big)}{\exp\Big(\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{n}B_{ij}w_{j}\Big)+\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{n}B_{ij}w_{j}\Big)},
(74)
where w_{j}=z_{1j}-z_{2j}. A similar calculation gives
\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(X_{i}=2|\mathbf{Z}=\mathbf{z})=\frac{\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{n}B_{ij}w_{j}\Big)}{\exp\Big(\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{n}B_{ij}w_{j}\Big)+\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{n}B_{ij}w_{j}\Big)}.
Thus, instead of using the 2n dimensional Gaussian {\mathbf{Z}}, one can use the n dimensional Gaussian W, and iterate between (73) and (74), This is the same exact algorithm, but we work with a lower dimensional representation of the auxiliary variable, which helps in faster computations. We note that this is the exact same algorithm as (Martens and Sutskever, 2010) in the Ising case.
C.2 Low rank Auxiliary Gaussian algorithm
Setting \mathbf{W}:=\mathbf{Z}_{1}-\mathbf{Z}_{2} as before, using (13) under \mathbb{Q} we have
\displaystyle(\mathbf{W}_{j}|\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{x})\sim N(\mathbf{p}_{j}^{\prime}(\mathbf{y}_{1}-\mathbf{y}_{2}),2/\mu_{j}),
(75)
with (W_{1},\ldots,W_{k}) mutually independent.
Also, using (14), we have
\displaystyle\mathbb{Q}(X_{i}=1|\mathbf{Z}=\mathbf{z})=
\displaystyle\frac{\exp\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{k}\mu_{j}z_{1j}p_{ji}\Big)}{\exp\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{k}\mu_{j}z_{1j}p_{ji}\Big)+\exp\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{k}\mu_{j}z_{2j}p_{ji}\Big)}
\displaystyle=
\displaystyle\frac{\exp\Big(\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{k}\mu_{j}w_{j}p_{ji}\Big)}{\exp\Big(\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{k}\mu_{j}w_{j}p_{ji}\Big)+\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{k}\mu_{j}w_{j}p_{ji}\Big)},
(76)
where w_{j}=z_{1j}-z_{2j}. A similar calculation gives
\displaystyle\mathbb{Q}(X_{i}=2|\mathbf{Z}=\mathbf{z})=\frac{\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{k}\mu_{j}w_{j}p_{ji}\Big)}{\exp\Big(\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{k}\mu_{j}w_{j}p_{ji}\Big)+\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{k}\mu_{j}w_{j}p_{ji}\Big)}.
Thus, instead of using the 2k dimensional Gaussian {\mathbf{Z}}, one can use the k dimensional Gaussian W, and iterate between (75) and (76).

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile
support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the
methods listed below:
Click the "Report Issue" (
) button, located in the page header.
Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.
Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we
may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability
should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for
all.
Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
